Operative Procedure: 
Sterile technique was used throughout the case. All vascular access was obtained using modified Seldinger technique by the cardiology team. A 5F sheath was placed in the right femoral artery and another inferior to the original one and a 6F sheath was placed in the right femoral vein. Next, a temporary pacing wire was placed in the right ventricle via the venous sheath using fluoroscopic guidance. The active fixation lead was placed in the right ventricle with appropriate capture threshold of 0.30 mA. A 5F pigtail catheter was placed in the RFA sheath and positioned in the non coronary cusp. The patient was evaluated for Sentinel embolic protection however judged not to be a candidate due to large innominate vessel size (18mm diameter in maximal dimension). 
The 5F sheath in the right femoral artery was removed and the arteriotomy was preclosed with 1 Perclose. After preclosure, the access site was upsized directly to a 16 Fr-Esheath delivery sheath over a Lunderquist wire. I joined the table.  After securing the delivery sheath, a 5F AL1 was advanced to the aortic root. Using a 0.035" straight
wire, the aortic valve was crossed. Over the wire, the AL1 catheter was advanced across the valve. The straight wire was removed and exchanged for a preformed Amplatz Extrastiff J wire. Next, the Edwards Sapien S3 delivery system with a mounted valve was delivered to the ascending aorta. After confirming appropriate placement across the aortic valve using aortic root angiogaphy, the 29mm [NAME] valve was deployed with rapid ventricular pacing at 180 bpm with Nominal volume -3cc. 
 
Following valve deployment, the transthoracic echocardiogram and aortic root angiogram revealed a well placed and well seated valve, but with some aortic regurgitation. We then postdilated the valve with rapid ventricular pacing in the usual manner at nominal volume -2cc in the delivery balloon. Following this, transthoracic echocardiogram and aortic root angiogram showed improvement in the aortic regurgitation to trivial regurgitation. 
 
The delivery catheter system was removed. The right femoral artery superior access site was closed using the predeployed 1 Perclose and 1 8F VIP Angioseal. A sheath injection angiography of the right femoral artery showed normal flow without significant stenosis, dissection, or contrast extravasation. I left the table.  The right femoral artery inferior access site was successfully closed using manual compression for inferior sheath. The remaining sheaths in the femoral arteries and/or veins were pulled and manual compression hemostasis applied. The patient tolerated the procedure well.

OPERATIVE PROCEDURE: The patient was taken to the operating room, placed supine on the operating table. After successful induction of general endotracheal anesthesia and placement of hemodynamic monitoring catheters, the chest and legs were prepped in standard fashion for cardiac surgery. 1.5 lengths of saphenous vein were harvested endoscopically from the leg, and meanwhile, the sternum was opened in the midline and the left internal thoracic artery was held harvested in skeletonized fashion from the chest wall. 
The thymus was divided between ties, the pericardium opened and the heart and great vessels exposed.  The aorta was palpated and found to be free from significant atherosclerotic disease.  The patient was
systemically heparinized and cannulated in the ascending aorta and right atrium for cardiopulmonary bypass.  A retrograde cardioplegia cannula was placed in the coronary sinus.  After achievement of an adequate ACT the patient was placed on systemic cardiopulmonary bypass and an antegrade cardioplegia needle was placed in the ascending aorta. 
The aorta was crossclamped and the heart arrested with a single dose of cold blood cardioplegia antegrade and retrograde.  During the cross-clamp period cardioplegia was delivered every
15 minutes. After achievement of adequate diastolic arrest, anastomoses were performed as follows:the PDA was identified.  This was a large vessel.  A length of vein was sewn to this with running 7-0 Prolene end to side.  Cardioplegia was delivered down the graft.  Next the OM was examined.  This was a very small vessel with diffuse calcification.  We elected not to graft it.  The first diagonal was a large vessel with mild diffuse disease.  A second length of vein was used for this vessel. 
The left internal thoracic artery artery was anastomosed to the left anterior descending with running 7-0 Prolene suture.  The LAD was a large diffusely diseased vessel.  Following completion of this anastomosis the ascending aorta was opened and the valve exposed.  The valve was trileaflet and quite sclerotic.  The leaflets were more thickened and fibrotic than calcified.  A 25 mm valve was chosen.  This was sutured in place with 15 interrupted pledgetted mattress sutures with pledgets on the ventricular side.  The aortotomy was closed with running 4-0 Prolene.  2 proximal anastomoses were formed to the ascending aorta after carefully measuring the grafts to length. 
A hot shot of retrograde and antegrade cardioplegia was delivered and the cross-clamp removed with return of normal sinus rhythm.  Ventilation was resumed and the patient was weaned from cardioplegic bypass with minimal inotropic
support. 
[NAME] was administered cannulas were removed from the heart and all cannulation sites doubly oversewn with 4-0 Prolene suture.  After achievement of adequate mediastinal hemostasis and placement of ventricular pacing wires the sternum was closed with interrupted stainless steel sternal wires, [NAME] suture to the fascia and absorbable suture to the skin.

The patient was taken to the operating room and general

valve exposed.  The leaflets were resected and the annulus decalcified.  The valve
was trileaflet with heavily calcified leaflets.  The root and left ventricle were
irrigated.  Based on sizing, a 21-mm Trifecta bioprosthesis was selected.  This was
implanted utilizing 2-0 pledgeted braided stitches and placed in a mattress fashion
with the pledgets ventricular based.  The valve seated well below the ostia of the
coronary arteries.  The root and left ventricle were irrigated and the aortotomy
closed in 2 layers utilizing pledgeted 4-0 Prolene.  The aortic root was de-aired
and the cross-clamp released with the patient in Trendelenburg position.  The heart
began to beat spontaneously and returned to sinus rhythm.  Ventricular pacing wires
were placed and a chest tube was placed.  Lungs were ventilated and de-airing
assured utilizing echocardiographic guidance.  Once the heart was adequately de-
aired, cardiopulmonary bypass was weaned without difficulty.  [LOCATION] function
was good and bioprosthetic valve was functioning well.  The heart and aorta were
decannulated and protamine administered.  Hemostasis was achieved.  The pericardium
and pleural fat pads were approximated over the aorta.  The sternum was
reapproximated with wire.  The fascial and subcutaneous layers of the chest were
approximated with absorbable suture and the skin edges approximated.

well.

Right radial artery access was obtained and a 5/6F slender sheath was placed in the right radial artery. Over a [LOCATION] wire, a Sentinel embolic protection device was deployed.   
The 5F sheath in the right femoral artery was removed and the arteriotomy was preclosed with 1 Perclose. After preclosure, the access site was upsized directly to a 16 Fr-Esheath delivery sheath over a Lunderquist wire. I joined the table.  After securing the delivery sheath, a 5F AL1 was advanced to the aortic root. Using a 0.035" straight wire, the aortic valve was crossed. Over the wire, the AL1 catheter was advanced across the valve. The straight
wire was removed and exchanged for a preformed Amplatz Extrastiff J wire. Next, the Edwards Sapien S3 delivery system with a mounted valve was delivered to the ascending aorta. After confirming appropriate placement across the aortic valve using aortic root angiogaphy, the 29mm [NAME] valve was deployed with rapid ventricular pacing at 180 bpm with nominal volume -1.5cc. Following valve deployment, the transthoracic echocardiogram and aortic root angiogram showed a well placed and well seated valve, but with 1+ aortic regurgitation. We postdilated the valve with rapid ventricular pacing with nominal volume -1cc added to the delivery balloon and subsequent echo and aortogram confirmed improvement in the aortic regurgitation to trivial. 
Next, the delivery catheter system was removed. The Sentinel embolic protection device was removed over the Whisper J wire. The right femoral artery superior access site was closed using the predeployed 1 Perclose and 1 Angioseal. A sheath injection angiography of the right femoral artery showed normal flow without significant stenosis, dissection or contrast extravasation. I left the table. OPERATIVE PROCEDURE:
An 8 cm incision was made over the upper sternum.  The sternum
was divided from the sternal notch down into the right fourth intercostal space.  The thymus was divided and the pericardium was opened.  The ascending aorta was
palpated.  It was without evidence of atherosclerosis.  The patient was heparinized.  The distal ascending aorta was cannulated.  The right atrium was cannulated with a
two-stage venous cannula and a retrograde cardioplegia cannula placed in the
coronary sinus via the right atrium.  An antegrade cardioplegia cannula/aortic vent
was placed in the ascending aorta.  The patient was placed on cardiopulmonary
bypass.  The ascending aorta was cross-clamped and the heart was
arrested with cold
blood cardioplegia.  An aortotomy was performed.  The aortic valve leaflets were
excised.  The annulus was debrided.  The left ventricle and aortic root were then
copiously irrigated to remove any debris.  The [ADDRESS] Jude Trifecta aortic valve
was then sutured in place with pledgeted 2-0 sutures.  The pledgets were placed on
the ventricular side.  The valve seated well.  The aortotomy was closed in 2 layers
first with a running horizontal 4-0 Prolene, then a running 0 and 4-0 Prolene.  The
hotshot dose cardioplegia was given.  The heart and ascending aorta were de-aired
and the aortic cross-clamp was removed.  When the patient's heart was adequately
recovered and thoroughly de-aired, she was weaned from cardiopulmonary bypass
without difficulty.  Intraoperative transesophageal echo demonstrates similar
ventricular function and a well-functioning bioprosthetic aortic valve.  All
cannulas were removed and the heparin effect was reversed with protamine.  Hemostasis was obtained.  Chest drains and pacing wires were placed and the wounds

brought to the Intensive Care Unit in stable condition.

 part. The arch was calcified. The distal ascending aorta was slightly

 trileaflet and had redundancy of all 3 leaflets with moderate calcification.
 All the tissues were extremely fragile.
 Intraoperative transesophageal echocardiography preoperatively confirmed the
 above-mentioned findings and showed 1 to 2+ mitral regurgitation. Therefore,

 OPERATIVE PROCEDURE: Median sternotomy was performed. Left internal thoracic
 artery dissected from chest wall. The thymus was divided. Pericardium was
 opened. The ascending aorta was palpated. No evidence of
 atherosclerosis. The patient was heparinized. Distal ascending aorta was
 cannulated. Superior vena cava and inferior vena cava were cannulated in
 standard bicaval fashion, and an antegrade cardioplegia cannula/aortic vent was
 placed in the ascending aorta. The patient was placed on cardiopulmonary
 bypass. The bipolar clamp was placed around the right- sided pulmonary
 veins, and 8 applications were made. The ascending aorta was cross- clamped.

 The heart was arrested first with antegrade and then with retrograde cold
 blood cardioplegia. During the remainder of the cross-clamp period, cold
 blood cardioplegia was given every 15 minutes. Right atriotomy was performed after
 tapes were placed around the SVC and IVC, and a retrograde
 cardioplegia catheter was inserted directly into the coronary sinus and
 secured with a pursestring. The bipolar clamp was placed around the
 left-sided pulmonary veins and 8 applications were made.

 A 45 mm left atrial appendage occlusion clip was placed at the base of the
 appendage and seated nicely. The aortotomy was then performed.

 The aortic valve was inspected. The findings were as noted above.

 The aortic valve leaflets were excised. The annulus was debrided.

 Left ventricle and left ventricular outflow tract were copiously
 irrigated to remove all the debris.

 A 25-mm St. Jude Trifecta GT bovine pericardial aortic valve was sutured into place with pledgeted 2- 0 Ethibond stitches.
 Pledgets were placed on ventricular side. The valve seated well.

 The aortotomy was closed with double running 4-0 Prolene stitch. In situ left
 internal thoracic artery was then used to bypass the LAD. This
 anastomosis was done with running 7-0 Prolene suture. Prior to
 completing this, it was probed and found to be widely patent. The heart and ascending
 aorta were de-aired. The aortic cross-clamp was removed. Heart was
 allowed to re-perfuse, during which time, we performed the right-sided
 ablation using the bipolar clamp from the incision to the superior vena cava
 then the incision down to the inferior vena cava.
 Given the fragility of his tissues, we did not do a formal full
 Cox-Maze 4 procedure. Right atriotomy was closed with running 4-0 Prolene stitch.

 When the patient's heart had adequately recovered and thoroughly
 de-aired, he was easily weaned from cardiopulmonary
 bypass. Intraoperative transesophageal echocardiography demonstrated similar
 ventricular function and a well-functioning bioprosthetic aortic
 valve with 1+ mitral regurgitation. All cannulas were then removed.
 The heparin effect was reversed with protamine. Hemostasis was
 obtained. Chest drains and pacing wires were placed. Wounds were
 closed in standard fashion. He tolerated the procedure well. He
 will be brought into Intensive Care Unit in stable condition. Following
 procedure, his family will be updated about the patient's condition in
 the operating room.

He did well until [DATE] when he underwent bypass surgery for what was thought to be an acute coronary syndrome.  At that time he received a left internal mammary artery graft to the anterior descending coronary artery and a graft to the circumflex and the right coronary artery.  He had known mild to moderate aortic stenosis at that time but the valve was left alone because of evidently concerns about bleeding.  Unfortunately, now he has severe aortic stenosis and needs another operation.  The procedure was as follows. 

OPERATIVE PROCEDURE:
Under adequate general anesthesia the patient was prepped and draped in the usual fashion.  We dissected out the axillary artery and dissected out the femoral vein.  We were able to reopen the sternum without incident.  As we anticipated, the scarring was very
dense and it took us quite a white to get all the structures freed up.  There was a small plastic membrane that had been left anterior to the right ventricle.  When we got to the point that we could cross clamp the aorta we heparinized and cannulated the axillary artery, then the femoral vein, and the superior vena cava. We could not dissect out the left side of the heart to be able to get at the patent ITA graft.  We then went onto cardiopulmonary bypass and we cooled down to 22 degrees in order to protect the myocardium. We did cross clamp the aorta and we were able to use antegrade and retrograde blood cardioplegia intermittently throughout.  We did mostly retrograde.  We opened the aorta with an oblique aortotomy and excised the valve.  There was continuous backflow from the left main coronary artery based on the ITA graft that made the operation difficult to do.  After we decalcified the aortic root we used horizontal mattress sutures of 2-0 Tycron backed with Teflon felt to insert a #23 bovine pericardial heterograft.  When that was tied down we closed the aorta with two layers of 4-0 Prolene.  It had been necessary to disconnect the right coronary artery graft in order to get at the aortic valve and so we then did a proximal anastomosis of a vein graft.  We began rewarming and the hot shot was given.  The air was removed from the cardiac chambers and the cross clamp was removed from the aorta.  While the heart was regaining a spontaneous heart beat we did an interposition anastomosis to the previous vein graft to the right coronary artery which is really a pretty small graft.  Once we had rewarmed, a process that took quite some time because he is a very big man, the patient was weaned off cardiopulmonary bypass without difficulty.  The Protamine was given and the cannulae removed from the heart.  When complete hemostasis was obtained, again a process that took some time, two sponge counts and bulldog counts
were reported as correct, the chest was closed in the usual fashion.

The patient was prepped and draped in normal sterile fashion.  Median sternotomy was performed.  The
patient was heparinized and aortic and bicaval
cannulation was carried out.  Cardiopulmonary bypass was initiated.  The ascending
aorta was cross-clamped and the heart arrested with antegrade and retrograde
cardioplegia.  A proximal aortotomy was performed.  The aortic valve was found as
described as well as the abnormal coronary anatomy.  The aortic valve cusps were
removed and the annulus carefully debrided.  Generous irrigation was performed
repeatedly.  We then went to the right atrium and closed the ventricular septal
defect from the right side.  The defect was closed with 3 pledgetted sutures.  The
tricuspid valve tested competent.  Returning to the aorta, the aortic valve was
replaced with a Carpentier-Edwards pericardial valve #27, inserted with fourteen 2-0
Ethibond annular sutures.  We had to take the valve out once to get the perfect
orientation so that none of the coronaries was obstructed by a strut.  The aortotomy
was closed with running 4-0 Prolene.  The right atrium was closed with running 4-0
Prolene.  Cardioplegia hotshot was given.  The aortic cross-clamp was removed.  Pacing wires were placed.  The patient was weaned from cardiopulmonary bypass.  The
heart was decannulated.  Protamine was given.  Careful hemostasis was carried out.  Mediastinal chest tubes were placed.  The sternotomy was closed in an ordinary

prosthesis and no residual ventricular septal defect.

All vascular access was obtained using modified Seldinger technique by the cardiology team. 5F sheaths were were placed in the left femoral vein and the right and left femoral arteries. A temporary pacing wire was placed in the right ventricle via the left femoral vein sheath. A 5F pigtail catheter was placed in LFA and positioned in the non-coronary cusp.  The 5F sheath in the right femoral artery was removed and the arteriotomy was preclosed with one [NAME] device. I scrubbed and joined the case. 
After securing the delivery sheath, a 5F AL1 was advanced to the aortic root. Using a 0.035" straight wire, the aortic valve was crossed. Over the wire, the AL1 catheter was advanced across the valve. The straight wire was removed and exchanged for a preformed Amplatz Extrastiff J-wire. Following valve deployment, the transthoracic echocardiogram and aortic root angiography demonstrated a well-placed and well-seated valve, with no more than mild significant aortic regurgitation. 
Next, the delivery catheter system was removed. The right femoral artery device access site was closed using the pre-deployed Perclose device and an 8F [NAME] by the cardiology team. A 5F pigtail catheter was then used for non-selective angiography of the iliofemoral system and showed normal flow without significant stenosis, dissection, or contrast extravasation. evidence of atherosclerosis.  The patient was heparinized.  The distal ascending
aorta was cannulated.  The right atrium was cannulated with a 2-stage venous
cannula, and a retrograde cardioplegia cannula was placed in the coronary sinus via
the right atrium.  An antegrade cardioplegia cannula/aortic vent was placed in the
ascending aorta.  The patient was placed on cardiopulmonary bypass.  The ascending
aorta was cross-clamped, and the heart was arrested with first antegrade and then
retrograde cold blood cardioplegia.  During the remainder of the cross-clamp period,
cold blood cardioplegia was given every 15-20 minutes.  A length of saphenous vein
graft was used to bypass the posterior descending artery.  A second length of
saphenous vein graft was used to bypass the diagonal, and the in situ left internal
thoracic artery was used to bypass the LAD.  All 3 distal anastomoses were
constructed with running 7-0 Prolene suture.  Prior to completing the anastomoses,
they were probed and found to be widely patent.  An aortotomy was performed.  The
aortic valve leaflets were excised.  The annulus was debrided.  The left ventricle
and aortic root were then copiously irrigated to remove any debris.  A 19-mm
Trifecta aortic valve was then sutured in place with pledgeted 2-0 sutures.  The
pledgets were placed on the ventricular side.  The valve seated well.  The aortotomy
was closed in 2 layers, first with a running horizontal 4-0 Prolene and then running
over-and-over 4-0 Prolene.  The proximal anastomoses of the 2 saphenous vein grafts
were constructed to the ascending aorta with running 6-0 Prolene suture.  A hotshot
dose of
cardioplegia was given.  The heart and the ascending aorta were de-aired,
and the aortic cross-clamp was removed.  When the patient's heart was adequately
recovered and thoroughly de-aired, she was weaned from cardiopulmonary bypass
without difficulty.  After being off cardiopulmonary bypass for a brief period of
time, she had a run of ventricular tachycardia.  We elected to put her back on
cardiopulmonary bypass for a few minutes and then she was weaned from
cardiopulmonary bypass.  Intraoperative transesophageal echo demonstrated similar
ventricular function and a well-functioning bioprosthetic aortic valve.  All
cannulae were removed and the heparin effect was reversed with protamine.  Hemostasis was obtained.  Chest drains and pacing wires were placed, and we began
closing the wound when the patient had severe episode of hypotension.  We were
unable to resuscitate her.  We therefore heparinized and once again placed her on
cardiopulmonary bypass.  We elected to place an intraaortic balloon pump.  We
dissected out the right femoral artery and inserted an intraaortic balloon pump
under transesophageal echocardiography guidance.  With the balloon pump functioning
well, the patient was weaned from cardiopulmonary bypass.  All cannulae were removed
and the heparin effect was reversed with protamine.  There was some dark venous
bleeding from the surface of the right atrium.  This was controlled with an
autologous pericardial patch that was sutured in place with a running 6-0 Prolene
suture.  After hemostasis was obtained, chest drains were placed.  The wounds were
closed in the standard fashion.  The patient tolerated the procedure and was brought
to the Intensive Care Unit in stable, but critical condition.

severe calcification of all 3 leaflets with lot of calcium around the annulus, and

thoracic artery, and she has usually anterior anatomy since that the LAD is occluded
at the level of very large
diagonal branch.  The diagonal is a dominant vessel in
that portion of the circulation and the LAD distally was small, so we opted to place
the left internal thoracic artery to the diagonal, put a vein in the distal LAD.  The left internal thoracic artery was taken as a skeletonized conduit and although
small, was of good caliber throughout the length needed to get to the diagonal.  The
vein was also of small caliber, but uniform in diameter.  The left atrial appendage
had a discrete base to it.  The rest of the findings were normal.  On intraoperative
TEE evaluated by both [LOCATION] and Cardiology, her mitral regurgitation was [DATE] at
most with a regurgitant orifice of 0.3, and so we opted to leave the mitral valve
alone. 

OPERATIVE PROCEDURE:
The patient was brought to the OR and placed on the table in
supine position.  Following the adequate induction of anesthesia and placement of
central venous and arterial monitoring lines, she was prepped and draped in the
usual fashion.  Median sternotomy was performed.  Left internal thoracic artery was
harvested in a skeletonized fashion by Dr. [NAME], while endoscopic vein harvest was
performed by Ms. [NAME].  Once the conduit was deemed adequate, she was heparinized
and cannulated via the ascending aorta and the right atrium again by Dr. [NAME], while
I was readily available.  I then scrubbed into the operating room.  We placed the
patient on full cardiopulmonary bypass.  The aorta was cross-clamped and the heart
was arrested with first antegrade followed by retrograde cold blood cardioplegia.  Intermittent dose of retrograde cold blood cardioplegia delivered throughout the
case as well as down the vein graft.  We first turned our attention to the distal
LAD, which was grafted in end-to-side fashion with a piece of vein.  The left
internal thoracic artery was then grafted in end-to-side fashion to the diagonal
artery.  We then opened the aorta above
the sinotubular junction, excised the valve,
debrided the annulus, irrigated the left ventricle copiously with warm saline.  I
then sized for a small [NAME] valve.  While the valve was being collapsed, we
performed the proximal anastomosis of the vein graft to the ascending aorta and
ligated the left atrial appendage with TigerPaw device.  The [NAME] valve was then
delivered into the aortic calcified root and deployed without difficulty.  The
balloon was used to confirm the valve to the annulus and then the aortotomy was
closed with running 5-0 Prolene sutures.  Hotshot dose of cardioplegia was given,
heart was de-aired.  Cross-clamp was removed.  Heart was allowed to reperfuse for a
bit, and she was easily weaned from cardiopulmonary bypass.  TEE confirmed preserved
biventricular function, adequate de-airing of the heart, and excellent valve
function with moderate mitral regurgitation, and really low gradients across her
aortic valve with no paravalvular leak.  The peak gradient of 13 mm and a mean
gradient of 7 mm across the aortic valve.  [NAME] were removed.  Heparin was
reversed with protamine.  Good hemostasis was confirmed.  [NAME] pacing wires
and mediastinal chest tube and left pleural chest tube were placed and then the
chest was closed in usual fashion by Dr. [NAME] while I was readily available.  The
patient was taken to the ICU in stable condition.

DESCRIPTION OF PROCEDURE: Informed consent was obtained.  The patient was brought to the hybrid room, a huddle was performed, anesthesia care was established, and intravenous antibiotics were given.  The patient was prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion.  To begin, vascular access was obtained by the Cardiology team members using sterile micropuncture technique and fluoroscopic and ultrasound guidance. In the groin, an 8-French sheath was placed superiorly and a 5-French sheath placed inferiorly in the right femoral artery.  A 6-French sheath was placed in the right femoral vein.  A temporary pacing wire was positioned in the right ventricle via the venous sheath and a 5-French straight flush catheter was positioned in the noncoronary cusp of the aortic valve. Right radial artery access was obtained and a 5/6F slender sheath was placed in the right radial artery. Over a [LOCATION] wire, a Sentinel embolic protection device
was deployed. 
The 8-French sheath in the right femoral artery was removed, the artery preclosed and the access site was upsized to a 14-Fr Esheath delivery sheath over a Lunderquist wire. I joined the table.  After securing the delivery sheath, a 5F AL1 was advanced to the aortic root. Using a 0.035" straight wire, the aortic valve was crossed. Over the wire, the AL1 catheter was advanced across the valve. The straight wire was removed and exchanged for a preformed Amplatz Extrastiff J wire. Next, the Edwards Sapien S3 delivery system with a mounted valve was delivered to the ascending aorta. After confirming appropriate placement across the aortic valve using aortic root angiogaphy, the 26mm [NAME] valve was deployed with rapid ventricular pacing at 180 bpm at nominal volume -2.5cc. Following valve deployment, the transthoracic echocardiogram and aortic root angiogram revealed a well-placed and well-seated valve. 
Next, the delivery catheter system was removed and the [LOCATION] was removed.  The ESheath was removed. The right femoral artery superior access site was closed using the predeployed 1 Perclose. A sheath injection angiography of the right femoral artery showed normal flow without significant stenosis, dissection, or contrast extravasation.  I left the table. The remaining sheaths were removed and manual compression hemostasis applied. Hemostasis was obtained at the right radial artery site with a Vasc Band. The patient tolerated the procedure well.

Minimally invasive aortic valve replacement with 23-mm Carpentier-Edwards bovine pericardial aortic valve. 

ANESTHESIA:

Aortic stenosis. 

POSTOPERATIVE DIAGNOSIS:

OPERATIVE INDICATIONS:
The patient is a gentleman with symptomatic aortic stenosis.  Echocardiography demonstrated severely calcified valve.  Coronary angiography demonstrated normal coronary artery. Left ventricular function was felt to be preserved.  The patient was referred for aortic valve replacement. 

OPERATIVE FINDINGS:
There were no pericardial adhesions or effusions.  The ascending aorta was soft without evidence of atherosclerosis.  The heart was of normal size and demonstrated adequate contractility.  The aortic valve was trileaflet and severely calcified. 

OPERATIVE PROCEDURE:
An 8-cm incision was made over the upper sternum.  The sternum was divided from the sternal notch down into the right fourth intercostal space.  The thymus was divided and the pericardium was opened.  The ascending aorta was palpated, it was without evidence of atherosclerosis.  Patient was heparinized.  The distal ascending aorta was cannulated.  The right atrium was cannulated with a 2-stage venous cannula, and a retrograde cardioplegic cannula was placed in the coronary sinus via the right atrium.  An antegrade cardioplegic cannula/aortic vent was placed in the ascending aorta.  The patient was placed on cardiopulmonary bypass.  The ascending aorta was cross-clamped and the
heart was arrested with first antegrade and then retrograde cold blood cardioplegia.  During remainder of the cross-clamp period, cold blood cardioplegia was given every 15-20 minutes.  An aortotomy was performed.  The aortic valve leaflets were excised.  [NAME] was debrided.  The left ventricle and aortic root were then copiously irrigated to remove any debris.  A 23-mm Carpentier-Edwards bovine pericardial aortic valve was then sutured in place with pledgeted 2-0 sutures.  The pledgets were placed on the ventricular side and the valve seated well.  The aortotomy was closed in 2 layers first with a running horizontal 4-0 Prolene and a running over-and-over 4-0 Prolene.  A hotshot dose of cardioplegia was given.  The heart and ascending aorta were de-aired and the aortic cross-clamp was removed. When the patient's heart was adequately recovered and thoroughly de- aired, he was weaned from cardiopulmonary bypass without difficulty. Intraoperative transesophageal echo demonstrated similar ventricular function and a well functioning bioprosthetic aortic valve.  All cannulas were removed and the heparin effect was reversed with protamine.  Hemostasis was obtained.  Chest drains and pacing wires were placed and the wounds were closed in standard fashion.  Patient tolerated the procedure well and was brought to the intensive care unit in stable condition.

Mediastinal and chest tubes.

GENETIC COUNSELING:
Transthyretin (TTR) amyloidosis is a condition in which abnormal protein deposits (amyloids) collect in specific organs, including the nervous system, eyes, and heart. In some cases it affects only the heart (TTR cardiac amyloidosis) and in some cases it affects multiple organs. TTR amyloidosis can be the result of a genetic condition (hereditary TTR amyloidosis) or it can be the result of normal protein that has abnormally deposited in the organ as a person ages (sometimes referred to as wild type amyloidosis).  Wild type amyloidosis (previously called senile amyloidosis) should be considered particularly in males over the [AGE]. 
It is important to determine if the abnormal protein is caused by a genetic problem or if it is the wild type form to help understand if other family members may be at risk for TTR amyloidosis.  Additionally, some
individuals with the genetic form have problems with other organs that might have been attributed to other conditions. 
Hereditary TTR amyloidosis is an autosomal dominant condition, meaning that one disease-causing variant in the TTR gene (heterozygous) predisposes a person to developing the disease. If an individual has hereditary TTR amyloidosis (a disease-causing variant in the TTR gene), all of their first degree relatives (parents, siblings and children) have a 50% risk of having inherited the same variant. Genetic testing of the TTR gene is able to identify a disease-causing variant in most individuals with hereditary TTR amyloidosis. 
Genetic testing should be started in a person who has amyloidosis. Identification of a disease-causing variant (pathogenic mutation) in TTR would confirm an underlying genetic cause for amyloidosis in the family and may provide useful information to help guide medical management. If a disease-causing variant is identified in a person with TTR amyloidosis, other family members could then consider testing for the familial variant to clarify their risk of developing the disease. In that case, family members who do not have the variant do not need to be clinically screened for amyloidosis. Family members with variants should be followed by a cardiologist and neurologist familiar with amyloidosis and additional specialists may also be recommended. Identification of a variant in family members without symptoms does not guarantee they will develop the disease, only that they have an increased risk. 
Sometimes, a variant of unknown significance is identified. In these cases, we will work with the patient to determine whether testing in other family members may help to clarify the results. Variants of unknown significance are not useful for assessing risk for asymptomatic family members.

OPERATIVE INDICATIONS:
The patient is an [AGE] gentleman with severe aortic
stenosis.  He is symptomatic and has shortness of breath.  Comorbidities include
hypertension, hyperlipidemia, chronic kidney disease, status post left nephrectomy.  I first reviewed his cardiac catheterization, which shows mild nonobstructive

severe aortic stenosis with 1-2+ aortic insufficiency.  His chest CT scan shows an

benefits of proceeding with surgery.  He agreed and wished to proceed. 

OPERATIVE FINDINGS:
There were no pericardial effusions or adhesions.  The
ascending aorta was soft without evidence of atherosclerosis.  The patient's heart

trileaflet and severely calcified.  Intraoperative transesophageal echocardiography
preoperatively confirmed the
above-mentioned findings. 

OPERATIVE PROCEDURE:
We started with a 6 cm right anterior thoracotomy overlying
the third rib.  This was taken down and the right chest was entered.  The mammary
was identified and clipped.  The third rib was disarticulated from the sternum and
we placed our soft tissue spreader and then soft tissue retractor and gentle rib
spreader.  The thymus was divided.  The pericardium was opened.  It became apparent
at this time that the exposure was extremely limited as we could not open up his rib
spaces more than about 4 cm.  His aorta would be also extremely challenging to
cannulate the distal ascending aorta from this approach.  We disarticulated the
second rib to see if this would allow us increased exposure and after
disarticulating this there was in fact no increased mobility.  The rib was actually
quite calcified as was the interspace, very small above it.  We decided at this
point it is safest to transition to a minimally invasive upper hemisternotomy
approach.  An upper hemisternotomy was then performed J-ing off to the fourth
interspace on the right.  The ascending aorta was palpated, had no evidence of
atherosclerosis.  The patient was heparinized.  Distal ascending aorta was
cannulated over a wire in Seldinger technique.  Right atrium was cannulated.  An
antegrade cardioplegia cannula/aortic vent was placed in the ascending aorta.  The
patient was placed on cardiopulmonary bypass.  The ascending aorta was cross-clamped
and the heart was arrested with 1 L of antegrade cold blood [LOCATION] cardioplegia.  An aortotomy was performed.  The aortic valve was inspected.  The findings were as

valve was sutured into place with
pledgeted 2-0 Ethibond stitches.  [NAME] were
placed on ventricular side.  The valve was seated well.  The aortotomy was closed
with double running 4-0 Prolene stitch.  Heart and ascending aorta were de-aired.  Aortic cross-clamp was removed.  The heart was allowed to re-perfuse for 5 minutes.  When the patient's heart had adequately recovered and thoroughly de-aired, he was
easily weaned from cardiopulmonary bypass.  Intraoperative transesophageal

bioprosthetic aortic valve with extremely low gradients.  All cannulas were then
removed.  The heparin effect was reversed with protamine.  Hemostasis was obtained.  Chest drains and pacing wires were placed and the sternotomy incision was closed in
usual fashion.  A minimally invasive right anterior thoracotomy approach was closed

back to the sternum.  He tolerated the procedure well.  He will be brought to
intensive care unit in stable condition.  Following the procedure, his family will
be updated about the patient condition in the operating room.

The patient is a [AGE] gentleman with severe aortic

ascending aorta was actually quite elongated and this likely would make a right
anterior
thoracotomy approach somewhat challenging.  Given this, we decided to do an
upper hemi-sternotomy.

I scrubbed and performed the surgery with assistance of Dr.  [NAME].  A 6-cm upper skin incision was performed.  Then an upper hemi-sternotomy

palpated without evidence of atherosclerosis.  The patient was heparinized.  The
distal ascending aorta was cannulated.  The superior vena cava was cannulated.  An
antegrade cardioplegia cannula/aortic vent was placed in the ascending aorta.  The
patient was placed on cardiopulmonary bypass.  The ascending aorta was cross-clamped
and the heart was arrested with 1 L of antegrade cold blood [LOCATION] cardioplegia

noted above.  The aortic valve leaflets were excised.  The annulus was debrided.  The left ventricle and left ventricular outflow tract were then copiously irrigated

was sutured into place with pledgeted 2-0 Ethibond sutures.  [NAME] were placed on

running 4-0 Prolene stitch.  Heart and ascending aorta were de-aired.  Aortic cross-
clamp was removed.  When the patient's heart had adequately recovered and was
thoroughly de-aired, he was weaned from cardiopulmonary bypass without difficulty.  Intraoperative transesophageal echocardiography demonstrated good ventricular
function and a well-functioning seated bioprosthetic aortic valve.  All cannulas
were therefore removed.  The heparin effect was reversed with protamine.  Hemostasis
was obtained.  Chest drains and pacing wires were placed.  The wounds were then
closed in
standard fashion.  He tolerated the procedure well.  He will be brought to
Intensive Care Unit in stable condition.  Following the procedure, his family will
